title: Trump Upends Saudi Nuclear Deal by Adding Abraham Accords Condition Hours After Signing
excerpt: The president blindsided his own nuclear negotiators by demanding Saudi Arabia normalise ties with Israel before the civilian nuclear agreement can proceed.
body:
• The US and Saudi Arabia signed a civilian nuclear cooperation agreement on July 22, but Trump added an Abraham Accords condition less than 24 hours later via social media.
  • The condition caught Trump's own nuclear negotiators off guard — the Abraham Accords requirement was not part of the signed deal.
  • Saudi Arabia has consistently said it will not normalise ties with Israel without a clear path to Palestinian statehood, which Netanyahu has rejected.
  • Nonproliferation experts warn the deal lacks sufficient safeguards against uranium enrichment for weapons purposes.

The Deal and the Reversal

On Wednesday, July 22, officials gathered at the Energy Department's headquarters in Washington for a ceremony two decades in the making: the signing of a civilian nuclear cooperation agreement between the United States and Saudi Arabia. Energy Secretary Chris Wright signed the deal while his Saudi counterpart joined from Riyadh via video link.

The Saudis had won much of their wish list. But the celebration was short-lived. By Thursday morning, Trump posted on Truth Social that the agreement was "totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords" — the initiative from his first term that led several Arab countries to normalise diplomatic relations with Israel.

Trump also denied the agreement would allow uranium enrichment, writing that the United States "is not opposed to Civil (Non-Enriched) Nuclear Facilities."

"Trump post bears almost no relation to what just got signed."

— Matt Bunn, Harvard University's Managing the Atom project

Chaos Inside the Administration

The Abraham Accords condition surprised Trump's own nuclear negotiators, CNN reported, citing two sources briefed on the matter. The president was reportedly angry that Wright had announced the deal without informing him first, and his frustration deepened after Fox News and the Wall Street Journal editorial page questioned why the agreement was struck without a normalisation component.

White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said at a briefing that the deal was "contingent on Saudi Arabia signing the Abraham Accords" but could not explain how that condition would be enforced, given that the Energy Secretary had already signed the agreement.

The Saudi Stalemate

The condition creates an immediate impasse. Saudi Arabia has consistently said it will not normalise relations with Israel without the establishment of a clear path to Palestinian statehood. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected Palestinian statehood as incompatible with Israel's security interests. The Saudi Embassy in Washington declined to comment on Trump's assertion.

The standoff effectively freezes a nuclear agreement that was supposed to go to Congress for review, raising questions about its legal status and whether US companies can proceed with plans to build and operate nuclear power plants on Saudi soil.

Nonproliferation Concerns

Even before Trump's reversal, experts had raised alarms about the deal's safeguards. CNN reported that the draft accord does not require Saudi Arabia to forgo uranium enrichment or adopt the more intrusive IAEA monitoring arrangements that Congress has repeatedly demanded — the so-called "Gold Standard" that the US applied in its nuclear cooperation agreement with the UAE.

Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has previously said Saudi Arabia would develop its own nuclear weapons if Iran acquires the bomb. The Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists warned that the agreement "risks a Middle East arms race."

What's Next

The deal's future hinges on whether Trump enforces the Abraham Accords condition or quietly walks it back. With Saudi-Israeli normalisation nowhere close, the nuclear agreement may remain in limbo indefinitely. Congressional scrutiny is expected regardless, with bipartisan concerns about proliferation risks ensuring the agreement faces a tough road even without the Abraham Accords complication.
